explain.say: On 1 December 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks, a seamstress and experienced activist, refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger and was arrested. Watch the chain. Overnight Jo Ann Robinson's women's group printed thousands of leaflets, and Black citizens stayed off the buses for 381 days, until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation illegal.

explain.say: The boycott made a young pastor, Martin Luther King Junior, famous. Look at the timeline. The March on Washington in 1963, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and at Selma in March 1965 police beat peaceful marchers on a bridge, Bloody Sunday. Within months the Voting Rights Act protected Black Americans' right to vote. Why did television pictures of Selma matter so much?

explain.say: Ideas travel. Look at the network. King studied Gandhi's satyagraha, nonviolent resistance, and visited India in 1959. In 1963 Bristol's Black residents boycotted a bus company that refused to hire them. Northern Ireland's marchers sang the American anthem We Shall Overcome, and in India the Dalit Panthers took their name from America's Black Panthers. Can you trace one link?

nodes.label: Gandhi's satyagraha
nodes.ask: How did the civil rights movement spread around the world?

explain.say: Now the map. Australia's 1965 Freedom Ride exposed racism in country towns, and in 1967 over 90 percent of voters backed changing the constitution for Aboriginal people. India's 1950 constitution, chaired in drafting by B. R. Ambedkar, abolished untouchability. Each movement fought its own injustice, but borrowed courage from others. Which place surprises you?

Now the historians. The classic story centres on Dr King from 1954 to 1968; Jacquelyn Dowd Hall's long civil rights movement stretches from the 1930s and stresses women and local organisers like Ella Baker. Great work. Exam tip: show both leaders and grassroots, and say what changed in law and in life.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Leaders mattered; so did thousands of organisers.

faq.q: What was the Montgomery bus boycott?
faq.a: After Rosa Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955 for refusing to give up her seat, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, boycotted the city buses for 381 days. The Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional, and the boycott ended in December 1956.

faq.q: What did the Voting Rights Act do?
faq.a: Passed in August 1965 after the Selma marches, it banned literacy tests and other devices used to stop Black Americans voting and sent federal officials to register voters. Black voter registration in the South rose sharply.

faq.q: How did the civil rights movement spread around the world?
faq.a: Ideas of nonviolent resistance went from Gandhi to the US movement, and American tactics and songs inspired the Bristol bus boycott of 1963, Australia's 1965 Freedom Ride, Northern Ireland's civil rights marches and India's Dalit Panthers.
asks: What was the Bristol bus boycott?

faq.q: Who led the civil rights movement?
faq.a: Martin Luther King Jr. was its best-known leader, but it relied on many others: Rosa Parks, Ella Baker, John Lewis, Fannie Lou Hamer, Bayard Rustin, Jo Ann Robinson, students in SNCC and thousands of local organisers, many of them women.

faq.q: What is the long civil rights movement?
faq.a: An approach, set out by historian Jacquelyn Dowd Hall in 2005, that extends the movement back to the 1930s and forward into the 1970s, includes the North as well as the South, and stresses jobs, housing and grassroots organisers.
asks: What did Jacquelyn Dowd Hall argue?

facts: Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery on 1 December 1955.
The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days.
The US Voting Rights Act was signed in August 1965.

quiz.say: The Montgomery boycott began on 5 December 1955 and lasted 381 days. Roughly how many weeks is that?
quiz.why: 381 divided by 7 is about 54 weeks, just over a year.

wrong.1: 38 weeks would be only about 266 days.

quiz.say: Which law followed the Selma marches of 1965?
quiz.why: The Voting Rights Act was signed in August 1965, months after Bloody Sunday.

wrong.1: Brown v. Board was a 1954 court ruling about schools.
wrong.2: The Chinese Exclusion Act was an 1882 immigration law.
